# Notes on Psalm 108 for a verse-by-verse commentary

**What I covered and what's missing.** I read Enduring Word (Guzik), Spurgeon on Blue Letter Bible and StudyLight, the Pulpit Commentary, Ellicott, the Bible Hub notes (Gill, Barnes, Cambridge, Geneva), Kretzmann (Lutheran) and Augustine on New Advent. My search budget ran out before I could get Wesley's notes, the NET Bible translator notes, Matthew Henry's full comments or any Pentecostal, Orthodox or prosperity-teaching sources. None of those are below. Among the sources I did read, I found **no real disagreement between Protestant traditions** on this psalm. The differences that do exist are between traditional and critical views of who wrote it, and between historical and Christ-centred readings.

## The psalm as a whole
- It's built from two earlier psalms: Psalms 108:1-5 being from Psalms 57:7-11; Psalms 108:6-13 being from Psalms 60:7-12. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-108.html
- Guzik (Calvary Chapel, on a Pentecostal-leaning site) says these are David's words, by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. https://enduringword.com/psalm-108-praise-and-trust-from-the-past-for-today/
- Barnes suggests the wholly triumphant tone may intimate that it was prepared by David, omitting the plaintive portions of the other Psalms. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/108-8.htm
- **Critical view:** Ellicott says giving this composite psalm to David furnishes a strong presumption against the historical value of the inscriptions. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-108.html
  - The Pulpit Commentary's homilies say the wording of v. 11 suggests that the psalm was rewritten by a returned exile, to whom the Captivity was a "casting off" of the nation by God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-108.html
- **Catholic (Augustine):** he didn't write a full exposition, because he had already covered Psalms 57 and 60. He argues that psalm titles which seem historical are most rightly understood prophetically. The two halves meet not in the surface of the history, but in the depth of prophecy. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801108.htm

## Verse by verse

**v. 1**
- Spurgeon reads "my heart is steadfast" as a settled resolve despite many wars and cares. He says God's grace has overcome the fickleness of nature. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/108-1.htm
- The Geneva Study Bible (Reformed) says this earnest feeling shows he is free from hypocrisy and that sluggishness does not stop him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/108-1.htm
- What "my glory" means is disputed:
  - Gill takes it as his tongue (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/108-1.htm).
  - Another note on the same page takes it as heart or soul, or as the tongue (citing Psalm 16:9 and Acts 2:26).
  - Cambridge takes it as my soul, the noblest part of me, but says it may be a scribe's addition taken from Psalm 57.
  - The Pulpit Commentary admits it is difficult to assign any distinct meaning to the last clause. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-108.html
  - Guzik says David praised God with the best of his being, including his musical skill. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-108/
- On the text itself: Psalm 57 repeats "my heart is steadfast," and here it is said once (Pulpit Commentary). The Septuagint and Vulgate restore the repetition, which is why the Prayer Book version reads "my heart is ready" twice (Cambridge, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/108-1.htm).

**v. 2**
- Guzik says David gave God the best part of the day: his praise greeted the dawn as it rose. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-108/
- A Pulpit homily notes that in Eastern usage, getting up early to do something showed real earnestness about it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-108.html

**v. 3**
- The text change here is "LORD" (Jehovah) where Psalm 57 has "Lord" (Adonai). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/108.htm
- Guzik says this praise was open and public, not secret. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-108/
- Bible Hub's chapter summary links the worldwide praise to the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19). https://biblehub.com/chaptersummaries/psalms/108.htm

**v. 4**
- Guzik explains "mercy" as *hesed*: loving-kindness, loyal love, covenant love. It is so great it would reach above the heavens if it could be measured. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-108/
- Kretzmann (Lutheran) says God's mercy goes beyond what humans can understand and his truth fills the whole universe. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/psalms-108.html
- Augustine on "above the heavens" versus Psalm 57's "unto the heavens": it is great unto the heavens, that it may be great in the heavens. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801108.htm

**v. 5**
- Guzik: since God's mercy and truth reach so high, the honour given to him should be just as great. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-108/
- He quotes Boice: The goal of history is that God might be known as God and be honored for it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-108/

**v. 6**
- Guzik: the praise turns into prayer, and David only mentions his trouble after setting his heart right. "Beloved" (*yadid*) echoes what David's own name means. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-108/
- A Pulpit homily says praise leads to prayer and gives confidence in prayer. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-108.html
- Another homily says believers may think of themselves, as David did, as God's beloved. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/108.htm
- Bible Hub's summary sees this plea as pointing forward to Christ's saving work (John 3:16). https://biblehub.com/chaptersummaries/psalms/108.htm

**v. 7**
- Cambridge on "in his holiness": "spoken" here means "promised" or "sworn." God's holy nature makes it impossible for Him to break His promise.
  - God is pictured as a victorious warrior dividing up the land.
  - Shechem stands for the land west of the Jordan and Succoth for the land east of it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/108-7.htm
- Spurgeon links this to God's large promises to David, which his holiness guaranteed. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps108.cfm
- In a sermon on this verse, Spurgeon calls God's word the foundation of faith. He also warns against treating God's promises as an excuse to do nothing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/108-7.html
- **Christ-centred reading:** a note gathered by Spurgeon reads the speaker as the second David, who gives out the nations: the Jew first and then the Gentile. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps108.cfm
- Augustine works from a Latin text that reads "I will be exalted." He takes the dividing of Shechem as prophecy of what follows the Lord's exaltation. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801108.htm

**v. 8**
- Cambridge: Gilead and Manasseh stand for the tribes east of the Jordan, Ephraim and Judah for those west of it. God claims all as His own: therefore all can claim God's protection.
  - Ephraim, the strongest tribe, is the helmet. Judah, David's royal tribe, is the sceptre, alluding to Genesis 49:10. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/108-8.htm
- Guzik cites Calvin (Reformed) for the same reading of Ephraim. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-108/
- Augustine reads Ephraim as "bearing fruit." "Taking up of my head" can mean we take up Christ, or Christ, the Head of the Church, takes us up. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801108.htm

**v. 9**
- Two readings of the sandal:
  - Cambridge's preferred reading: Moab is the washbasin brought to the returning warrior, and Edom is like the slave to whom the warrior flings his sandals.
  - The other reading: an Eastern custom of claiming land by throwing a shoe on it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/108-9.htm
- Guzik's comments:
  - Both nations were known for pride, and God gives them humble service.
  - The shoe shows contempt.
  - He links each line to David's conquests in 2 Samuel 8. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-108/
- The Pulpit Commentary says Psalm 60:8 reads "Philistia, triumph thou over me." Apparently the compiler has not understood David's irony. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-108.html

**v. 10**
- Guzik quotes Boice: "the fortified city" can only mean Petra, Edom's stronghold. Guzik adds there is no biblical record of David taking it, so it may stand for any city that looks unconquerable. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-108/
- Spurgeon applies it to some Petra-like evil in your soul. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/psalms-108.html

**v. 11**
- The Pulpit Commentary prefers the Revised Version's reading, "Hast not thou cast us off, O God?" https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/108.htm
- Guzik says the prayer comes after recent defeats, which happened because God's favour was not with the armies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-108/
- Spurgeon notes that the same man who feels cast off in v. 11 still rejoices in v. 7. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/psalms-108.html
- For the exile reading of this verse, see the Pulpit homily under "The psalm as a whole."

**v. 12**
- Guzik quotes VanGemeren: the king is not looking for alliances, because their help is worthless. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-108/
- He also quotes Spurgeon: Faith is neither a coward nor a sluggard. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-108.cfm
- Bible Hub's summary links the verse to Jeremiah 17:5. https://biblehub.com/chaptersummaries/psalms/108.htm

**v. 13**
- Guzik: Israel would still fight, but fight "through God." He quotes Spurgeon that God's working is not an argument for human inaction, and Morgan that this is ever the way of victory. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-108/
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary applies it to the Christian's spiritual warfare: If we would conquer we must be found in the way of duty. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/psalms-108.html
